adoption.body: Businesses in the Census Bureau's survey report current AI use at 21.8%. Expected use within six months is 25.9%, but the measure records stated intent rather than current use. Near-term expectations therefore remain close to the current-use base.
adoption.headline: Business AI intentions sit just above reported current use

compute.body: Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, with capacity utilization at 81.7%. Semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%, but utilization was lower at 72.2%. Output is rising in both industries, while the utilization gap indicates different pressure on installed capacity.
compute.headline: Compute output is growing under different capacity conditions

data_center.body: Available project records list 3,068 operating sites and 1,556 sites in development, a ratio of 0.51. Separately, 894 sites are tracked in the active pipeline. Meta is reportedly planning a further expansion of its Eagle Mountain campus in Utah, providing a current example of continued campus expansion without establishing the pace of the wider pipeline. These site counts describe the breadth of activity, not the power or compute capacity the projects will deliver.
data_center.headline: Project records show one development site for every two operating sites, with 894 sites tracked as active

finance.body: Operating cash flow is 1.42 times current CapEx, while cash reserves are equivalent to 0.96 years at the current spending pace. Borrower strain is 26.0, while lender strain is -13.5. The funding picture therefore combines cash-flow coverage above current CapEx with reserve coverage below one year and strain readings of opposite signs.
finance.headline: Cash flow covers current CapEx, but reserves alone fall short of a year

grid_storage.body: The active queue contains 2,061 GW, including 552.7 GW of storage, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Earlier experience cautions against reading the full queue as future operating supply: only 13% of the 2000–2020 queue cohort reached operation. That historical outcome is not a forecast for the current queue. Pennsylvania regulators are reportedly preparing to consider ratemaking, return on equity and curtailment as data-center load grows, putting pricing and operating rules alongside the physical buildout.
grid_storage.headline: The 2,061-GW grid queue remains mostly outside advanced stages

macro.body: Financial signals are mixed rather than uniformly weak. The AI Equity Index and average sector trading pressure edged lower, yet 61.3% of covered companies remain positive over one year and the median return increased to 14.8%. Operating cash flow equals 1.42 times current CapEx, while cash reserves equal 0.96 years of spending. Borrower strain is 26.0, compared with lender strain of -13.5. The funding picture combines support from current internal cash generation with a sub-one-year reserve cushion and divergent borrower and lender conditions. Physical expansion is visible in current output as well as project records. Computer and peripheral-equipment output grew 9.2%, and semiconductor and electronic-component output grew 11.5%. Data-center records show 0.51 development site per operating site, while 894 sites are tracked in the active pipeline. Yet only 24.2% of the 2,061-GW active interconnection queue is in executed-agreement or construction stages, and just 13% of the 2000–2020 cohort reached operation. The historical rate is not a forecast, but it cautions against treating proposed capacity as delivered supply. Pennsylvania regulators are reportedly considering ratemaking, returns and curtailment as data-center load grows, a reminder that grid expansion also requires decisions about prices and operating rules. Broad deployment remains gradual. Current AI use is reported by 23.2% of businesses, compared with 27.3% expecting use within six months, a 4.1-point gap. Only one tracked AI-linked labor channel has positive employment growth, and the strongest channel is growing 0.8%. Nonfarm-business productivity is growing 2.2%, but that aggregate does not identify an AI contribution. For now, the evidence is clearer on infrastructure activity than on broad labor-market or productivity effects.
macro.headline: Physical buildout continues, but pipeline conversion and broad deployment remain limited

market.body: The AI Equity Index slipped to 32.2 and average sector trading pressure to 50.0. The share of covered companies with positive one-year returns also edged down to 61.3%, but the median one-year return increased to 14.8%. The combination shows softer breadth without a uniform deterioration in company-level performance.
market.headline: Market indicators edge lower, but the median one-year return improves

power.body: Commercial electricity demand grew 3.0%, compared with 1.3% for total retail demand. Net planned generation additions edged up to 228.7 GW, but they remain a pipeline measure rather than delivered supply. Retail electricity prices rose 4.4%; that pace slowed materially, but prices are still increasing.
power.headline: Commercial power demand outpaces overall demand as price growth slows

editorial_briefing.style_reference: AI Macro is a research platform that examines the development of the U.S. AI economy from capital investment and physical construction through deployment, adoption, and economic results. It uses publicly available data to relate corporate and market activity to the physical systems required to support the buildout. It evaluates the extent to which that investment produces durable economic value and how its effects are transmitted through the broader U.S. economy.

The AI Equity Index and average sector trading pressure also declined slightly, to 30.9 and 48.8. These cases do not establish a failure rate for the wider pipeline, but they show why site counts should not be read as completed capacity.

paragraphs.text: Reported business use of AI increased to 23.8%, while 27.6% expect to use it within six months. The gap narrowed to 3.8 percentage points, putting stated near-term intentions closer to reported deployment, though expectations are not current use. Adoption is still uneven: the leading sector is at 49.0%, more than twice the all-business rate.

Physical project activity remains substantial. Available records show one development site for roughly every two operating sites—1,556 against 3,068—and separately track 894 active-pipeline sites. On the power side, the active interconnection queue totals 2,061 GW, but only 24.2% is in executed-agreement or construction stages. Recent reports of intensifying congestion from data-center load and an expanded Texas moratorium on data-center approvals show that connection and permitting can constrain project timing; they do not establish how much of the overall pipeline will fail.

Electricity and finance data explain why execution remains central. Commercial electricity demand grew 3.1%, versus 1.2% for total retail demand, while net planned generation additions stand at 225.2 GW and retail prices are rising 4.4%. Planned supply is not delivered capacity. The NFCI stands at -0.56, consistent with loose broad conditions, but borrower strain is 26.0 and CNBC reports that a bond-yield spike has increased risk for debt-hungry AI companies. Broad financial conditions can therefore coexist with funding pressure at firms most dependent on borrowing.
